.dt accessor: pandas' gateway to date parts: .dt.year, .dt.month, .dt.day_name(), etc.
.iloc: select rows/columns by integer position (starting at 0)
Central Limit Theorem: sample means become normally distributed as sample size grows, whatever the population shape
DataFrame: a table: many columns (Series) sharing one row index
IQR: Inter-Quartile Range = Q3 - Q1, the spread of the middle 50% of the data
KDE: Kernel Density Estimate — a smooth curve approximating the distribution
Law of Large Numbers: as sample size grows, the sample average converges to the true average
MAR: Missing At Random — gaps explained by OTHER observed columns
MCAR: Missing Completely At Random — gaps unrelated to anything
MNAR: Missing Not At Random — gaps depend on the missing value itself
NaN: 'Not a Number' — pandas' marker for a missing value
NaT: 'Not a Time' — the datetime version of a missing value
Type I error: false positive: rejecting a true null (rate = α)
Type II error: false negative: failing to reject a false null (rate = β); power = 1−β
Yeo-Johnson: an automatic power transform that symmetrizes data, allowing zeros/negatives
alpha (α): the significance threshold, usually 0.05; reject H0 when p < α
argument: an input value you pass into a function
array: NumPy's list-like container where every item is the same type, allowing whole-array maths
axis: the direction to collapse in a 2-D array: 0 = down rows (per column), 1 = across columns (per row)
bivariate: looking at the relationship between TWO variables
boolean: a value that is either True or False
boolean mask: an array of True/False used to filter another array
boxplot: a chart showing median, middle-50% box (IQR), whiskers, and outlier dots
broadcasting: NumPy auto-stretching a smaller array to combine with a larger one
cardinality: how many distinct values a categorical column has
categorical: a column whose values are labels/categories (like city or plan) rather than measured numbers
cell: one box in a notebook; either human text or runnable code
chi-square test: test for association between two categorical variables
churn: when a customer stops using / cancels a service — the thing we'll predict
confounder: a hidden variable that influences both things you see correlated, faking a link
copy: an independent duplicate; editing it does NOT affect the original
correlation: a number in [-1, 1] measuring linear association between two variables
data leakage: when info from test/target sneaks into training, inflating scores unrealistically
data type: the kind of a value: text (str), whole number (int), decimal (float), or True/False (bool)
dictionary: a collection accessed by name (key), written with { }
dtype: the data type of a column — int (whole number), float (decimal), object (usually text), datetime, or category
error / exception: Python's message telling you what confused it and where
feature: an input column the model learns from (age, income, ...)
for loop: code that repeats once for each item in a collection
function: a reusable mini-machine: inputs go in, an output comes back
groupby: split rows into groups, apply a calculation to each, combine the results
histogram: a bar chart of counts per value-range (bin) — shows a distribution's shape
if statement: code that runs only when a condition is True
import: the command that loads a library so you can use its tools
index: the row labels of a Series/DataFrame
library: a toolbox of ready-made code you import to reuse
list: an ordered collection accessed by position (index), written with [ ]
log transform: replacing x with log(x); compresses long right tails toward symmetry
matplotlib: Python's core plotting engine — powerful, draws anything
melt: reshape wide → long (one row per observation, the 'tidy' shape)
merge / join: combine two tables by matching a shared key column
missing value / NaN: an empty cell; pandas shows it as NaN ('Not a Number')
multicollinearity: when two+ features are strongly correlated with each other, destabilizing linear models
normal distribution: the symmetric bell curve, defined by its mean and std
np: the standard nickname for NumPy (from `import numpy as np`)
np.where: a vectorized if/else: np.where(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false)
null hypothesis (H0): the default 'nothing interesting here' assumption a test tries to disprove
one-hot encoding: a 0/1 column per category — for unordered (nominal) features
ordinal encoding: mapping ordered categories to integers 0,1,2 — only when order is real
p-value: probability of data at least this extreme IF the null hypothesis were true
pdf: Probability Density Function — the curve giving a distribution's shape
pivot_table: reshape long → wide (rows×columns grid), optionally aggregating
population: the entire group you care about (all customers ever)
print(): a command that displays a value on the screen
range(n): produces the numbers 0, 1, ..., n-1 — handy for looping n times
reshape: rearrange the same values into a new shape (total count must match)
return: the keyword that sends a function's result back to the caller
sample: the subset you actually measured (the customers in your data)
sampling distribution: the distribution of a statistic (like the mean) across many samples
scatter plot: dots plotting two numeric variables against each other to show their relationship
scikit-learn (sklearn): Python's main classic-ML library — models, scalers, encoders, and more
scipy.stats: Python's library of statistical distributions and tests
seaborn: a library built on matplotlib for quick, pretty statistical charts
seed: a fixed starting number that makes 'random' results repeatable
shape: the size of an array along each dimension, e.g. (rows, columns)
skew: lopsidedness of a distribution; positive = long right tail
snake_case: lowercase words joined by underscores, e.g. monthly_charges — the standard for column names
standard error (SE): the std of a sample statistic; for the mean, SE = std/√n
t-test: test comparing the means of two groups
traceback: the full error report; read the LAST line first
univariate: looking at ONE variable on its own
variable: a named box that stores a value you can reuse
vectorization: doing an operation on a whole array at once instead of looping element by element
vectorized (pandas): operating on whole columns at once (fast) instead of looping rows with .apply (slow)
view: a slice that shares memory with the original array (editing it edits the original)
z-score: how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean
